editions.title: Huang exit rattles Nvidia as Trump's Xi-Putin meeting is set
editions.notification: Nvidia shares slide after Jensen Huang quits as CEO; Colette Kress steps in as interim chief.
editions.intro:
Nvidia dominated the day after Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive, president and board member following reports of extramarital affairs, one reportedly involving a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The shares closed down just over 4% on Friday after falling as much as 14% in morning trading, and the stock has lost close to $1 trillion this month. Colette Kress is interim chief executive, Harvey Jones is the new independent chair, and the board has reportedly approached Arm's Rene Haas about the permanent role. The political fallout is spreading to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is accused of stalling action against Singapore's Megaspeed, and Democrats and Republicans are seeking answers.

Elsewhere, the White House confirmed that Donald Trump will meet Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, expected on 19 November, though a senior US official said no agreement is expected. Putin, meanwhile, signalled no compromise on Ukraine after meeting Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow. Europe agreed a five-nation group to speak for it in future talks.

Markets were also shaken by a global Microsoft 365 outage and a rare nationwide FAA ground stop that cancelled more than 6,700 US flights. On energy, the IEA says global oil supply has returned to surplus for the first time since the Iran war began, while Iran says two tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz.

editions.title: Nvidia's Huang out as CEO; Lutnick under fire
editions.notification: Jensen Huang has resigned as Nvidia CEO, wiping hundreds of billions off its value. Here is what it means for chips and Washington.
editions.intro:
The dominant story is Nvidia's leadership upheaval. Co-founder Jensen Huang has resigned as president, chief executive and director with immediate effect, after admitting affairs with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom US intelligence reportedly linked to China's Ministry of State Security, and with Nvidia vice-president Kimberly Powell. Colette Kress is interim chief executive and Harvey Jones is the first independent chair. Shares fell as much as 14% in early trading, and the company has lost up to $601 billion of value. The first results without Huang are due on 17 November.

The scandal is widening into US policy. Singapore has barred Alice Huang from re-entering the city-state, while saying US help in its Megaspeed probe was limited. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is reportedly under pressure from Congress and inside the White House after stalling export controls against Megaspeed, which CNN estimates bought more than $4bn of Nvidia chips. Commerce called reports of a clash with Treasury false. Trump has publicly backed Lutnick. Nvidia also privately told a lawmaker it could implement chip geotracking, which undercuts industry claims that such mandates are infeasible.

Beyond Nvidia, the day was dominated by fears for the AI trade. The Nasdaq fell more than 5% after Democrats' midterm gains raised the prospect of tougher AI and data-centre rules, wiping out over $2 trillion. Investors were not uniformly bearish: Nvidia largely recovered by Thursday's close, and Citi argued it is too early to call the AI trade structurally broken. OpenAI reportedly passed $10bn in quarterly revenue, though its losses widened, while Anthropic prepares its IPO next week.

editions.title: Jensen Huang quits Nvidia as CEO amid affair and China-spy scandal
editions.notification: Nvidia's Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO, wiping hundreds of billions off the chipmaker's value. Here's what it means.
editions.intro:
Nvidia's founder and chief executive Jensen Huang has resigned with immediate effect, ending a 33-year run that made the chipmaker the most valuable in the world. The board named chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive and Harvey Jones as its first independent chair. The exit follows reports of an affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom US intelligence reportedly suspects of spying for China, and a second relationship with a direct report. Nvidia's shares fell as much as 14% in early trading, pushing market value below $4 trillion and erasing up to $601 billion, which would be the largest one-day loss for any stock if it held at the close.

The fallout is spreading into politics and markets. Senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons have asked the administration to preserve records on Nvidia's China chip exports and on Huang's relationship, often a precursor to formal investigations. The New York Times reported that Trump had been warned about the relationship but took no action, and the Wall Street Journal reported that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick stalled action against Singapore-based Megaspeed, which may have funnelled chips to China. Trump has backed Lutnick publicly. Elsewhere, the tech sell-off hit broadly: the Nasdaq fell more than 5% on Thursday after Democrats' midterm gains raised fears of AI regulation and data-centre curbs.

The bigger question is what comes next. Nvidia reports quarterly results on 17 November, its first without Huang, and at least seven Wall Street firms have downgraded the stock this week. Anthropic's S-1 filing, which revealed rapid revenue growth and a claim that its models now run on AMD chips within days, adds pressure on Nvidia's software moat, while OpenAI reportedly passed $10bn in quarterly revenue. Investors will be watching the successor search and the governance fallout closely.

editions.title: Nvidia shares slide as reports of Jensen Huang's ouster mount
editions.notification: Nvidia shares tumble as reports say its board may move against CEO Jensen Huang. Here's what we know.
editions.intro:
The dominant story is Nvidia. Its shares fell more than 9.5 per cent over Monday and Tuesday and slid a further 7 to 8 per cent in after-hours trading on Wednesday, after the Wall Street Journal and New York Times reported that the board could meet as soon as the same day to decide the future of chief executive Jensen Huang. The reports follow Huang's admission of an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese intelligence agent, and a further alleged affair with Nvidia's vice president of health care, Kimberly Powell. Nvidia has hired former US attorney Joon H. Kim's firm to investigate, and US lawmakers have asked Huang to attend a closed-door briefing. Nvidia has not responded to comment requests, and the ouster reports remain unconfirmed rumours. Related chip stocks, including Korean memory makers and TSMC, are being watched for knock-on effects.

Elsewhere, the AI and chip economy kept generating deals. TSMC's board has reportedly approved up to $1 billion of investment in OpenAI and Anthropic, which would give the chipmaker direct stakes in two of its biggest customers, though analysts have flagged circular financing concerns. London chip designer Fractile raised $720 million at a $7 billion valuation, and South Korea's president said Samsung's packaging expansion could spur about $30 billion of further investment. Google DeepMind also unveiled AlphaProof Code, which formally verified the cryptographic core of Signal in four weeks.

On the consumer side, Google Wallet added digital home keys, Google Fi previewed a dual-carrier "super network", and reports suggest Grand Theft Auto VI has passed $1 billion in sales ahead of its 19 November release, a figure not yet confirmed by Take-Two. Regulators also acted: New York forced T-Mobile to drop data caps on low-income home internet plans, and Germany reportedly banned Chinese drones from military bases.

editions.title: Anthropic IPO talk builds as Nvidia's Huang faces FBI probe
editions.notification: Anthropic's IPO valuation talk climbs towards $1.5tn while Nvidia shares slide over the Huang probe.
editions.intro:
The biggest story of the period is the twin pressure on Nvidia and the surge of talk around Anthropic. Nvidia shares fell 4.3% on Monday, wiping roughly $190bn off its market value, after a class action accused the company and chief executive Jensen Huang of misleading shareholders over his alleged affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom US authorities reportedly concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia says it is running an independent investigation, and Donald Trump said the FBI was looking into the matter. Related reports tie Alice Huang to more than $7bn of Nvidia chip sales to China, which could strengthen bipartisan calls to tighten chip export controls.

Anthropic dominated the AI news. The Financial Times reports the company is considering an IPO at up to $1.4tn, with bankers reportedly preparing to lift the target to $1.5tn or more, and Goldman Sachs projects revenue above $600bn by 2030. These are rumours and forecasts, not confirmed plans. The company also released Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, with company-reported gains in coding and research and lower prices, and expanded Claude into a workspace with spreadsheets, whiteboards and data tools.

Elsewhere, AMD detailed its Zen 6 core and its Venice-X and Verano server chips, Alibaba's T-Head filed for a Hong Kong IPO, and the FCC is weighing a ban on Chinese optical transceivers that Microsoft is lobbying against. Regulation was also in focus, with a Paris Call on AI safety signed by ten AI companies but no deadlines or sanctions, and Australia recommending a new AI regulator after an OpenAI-linked breach.

editions.title: Nvidia's Huang scandal wipes $190bn as AI sell-off lingers
editions.notification: Nvidia loses $190bn in a day as CEO Jensen Huang faces an investigation over a China-linked affair.
editions.intro:
The dominant story is the scandal engulfing Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang. He has acknowledged an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, whom US officials reportedly concluded passed information to Chinese government channels. Nvidia's board has launched an independent investigation, Congress has asked for a briefing by 11 November, and a class action alleges shareholders were misled. Nvidia shares closed down 4.3% on Monday, wiping roughly $190bn from its market value. Reports also suggest Moonshot AI accessed top Nvidia chips in China despite export curbs, which, if confirmed, would sharpen the debate over export controls.

Elsewhere, the AI sector is moving fast. Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, with company-reported gains in speed and coding and lower prices, and reports say it is preparing a large IPO, with a valuation of up to $1.4tn. Google's Gemini 4 Carbon became generally available, and Meta launched a small, cheap model. Asian markets rebounded after a steep AI-led rout, while AMD forecast record revenue and said it expects to outsell Intel for the first time in a quarter.

Regulation and security also featured. Washington is weighing a ban on Chinese optical transceivers, which Microsoft is lobbying against, and the UK may widen its under-16 social media ban to marketplaces such as Vinted and eBay. Binance was reported to have lost $6.3bn in what Bloomberg calls the largest crypto heist on record.

BP and Shell each gained about 1.5% as crude rose after Houthi strikes on Saudi infrastructure and tanker attacks in the Gulf. Rate expectations are moving fast. Traders put the chance of another 25-basis-point Bank of England hike next month above 84%, and a Federal Reserve hike in December is also expected. That backdrop is pulling money into energy and insurers while growth-sensitive names lag.

Across the Atlantic the mood was less settled. Nvidia's leadership shock, which has wiped out nearly $1 trillion of value this month, weighed on US tech, yet the S&P 500 still rose 2.5% over the week. Asian chip stocks rallied anyway, and Europe had its best week since June.

World.summary:
The FAA lifted a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday evening after nearly five hours of disruption. Officials blamed a telecommunications failure linked to outdated equipment and said there was no sign of a cyberattack. More than 6,700 flights were cancelled and over 25,000 delayed, and Transport Secretary Sean Duffy now says the air traffic control upgrade needs $50 billion, not $30 billion, renewing calls for emergency funding. Airline shares fell, with JetBlue, American and United among the weakest.

Abroad, the White House has confirmed Donald Trump will hold a trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin at the APEC summit in Shenzhen on 19 November. A senior US official said no agreement is expected, and the agenda covers nuclear arms and Iran but not Ukraine. It comes after New START expired in February, leaving no major arms control framework.

Europe is focused on Ukraine. EU leaders agreed a five-nation group, the E5, to represent Europe in future peace talks, a response to fears of a Yalta-style deal. In the UK, Prime Minister Andy Burnham says a "win-win" deal with the EU could be done before next week's summit.

Tech.summary:
A global Microsoft 365 outage disrupted Outlook, Teams and other services on Friday 13 November, and Microsoft said its first fixes failed. The company blamed a process on affected servers that handles secure connections becoming overwhelmed, and it is rolling back a recent configuration change. Executive Charles Lamanna said there was no sign of malicious activity. In Australia, government agencies, courts and some clinics reported email problems, and authorities warned of scams exploiting the confusion.

The biggest new story in tech is therefore a reliability failure rather than a product launch. It shows how much of public-sector and business communication now depends on a single cloud provider. Microsoft's shares were down as a result.

Elsewhere, SpaceX's Starship flew its 15th test but the booster catch was aborted, leaving the double catch unfinished. The Ship continues in orbit, with a tower-catch decision expected on Saturday. Nvidia's leadership crisis also continues, with the chip-smuggling and China questions now reaching the White House.

Nvidia's co-founder Jensen Huang has resigned as president, chief executive and board member with immediate effect, ending a 33-year run that made the chipmaker worth roughly $4 trillion. The board has named chief financial officer Colette Kress interim chief executive and Harvey Jones as its first independent chair. The exit follows reports of relationships with a woman US intelligence reportedly linked to China's Ministry of State Security and with a direct report, and the shares fell as much as 14% in early trading.

The fallout is spreading across the sector. Democratic senators have asked the administration to preserve records on Nvidia's China chip exports, and reports say the Commerce Department stalled action against Megaspeed, a Singapore firm suspected of routing chips to China. Investors are now focused on Nvidia's third-quarter results on 17 November, the first without Huang, and on whether the AI boom's financing web, which Huang helped build, holds up.

Beyond Nvidia, the sector is under pressure from a broad tech sell-off, AI-linked concerns in US midterm politics, and a heavy pipeline of listings. Anthropic's S-1 filing shows revenue growing very fast, while OpenAI reportedly passed $10bn in quarterly revenue, though with much larger losses.

Fashion.title: Burberry rebounds as Capri names new CEO
Fashion.notification: Burberry swings back to profit as Capri names a new chief executive and luxury looks for growth beyond China.
Fashion.summary:
The biggest story in fashion and luxury today is the Nvidia governance shock, though it sits at the edge of the sector, not inside it. Reports say chief executive Jensen Huang has resigned after claims of extramarital relationships, one with a suspected Chinese agent, and Nvidia shares fell more than 11%. Within luxury, the clearest good news came from Burberry, which swung back to a £54m first-half profit on 6% revenue growth, with wholesale up 17% and the Americas up 12%.

Leadership change is a theme across the sector. Capri has named Estée Lauder veteran Justin Boxford as chief executive from 4 January, ending John Idol's long run, while Tod's has parted ways with creative director Matteo Tamburini. Burberry's Daniel Lee profile and Zimmermann's expansion plans add to the picture of brands leaning on creative direction and new markets.

Demand is the underlying worry. Luxury groups are reportedly turning to the United States as the Chinese growth engine stalls, and Gulf shoppers are cutting back as war-linked inflation bites. Coach and Ralph Lauren are reportedly bucking China's slump, while On Holding posted record sales and margins, helped by tariff refunds.

Finance.title: Energy and defensive stocks lift London as AI jitters grow
Finance.notification: FTSE 100 hits a three-month high as oil majors gain, while markets price in a Bank of England hike.
Finance.summary:
London's FTSE 100 closed at its highest level since early August on Friday, rising 0.4% as energy and defensive shares led while a wobble in global AI stocks pushed investors towards safer sectors. BP and Shell each gained about 1.5% as crude rose after Houthi strikes on Saudi infrastructure and tanker attacks in the Gulf. Aviva jumped 3.4% after reporting a 19% rise in general insurance premiums for the first nine months of 2026.

Rate expectations are moving fast. Traders put the chance of another 25-basis-point Bank of England hike next month above 84%, and a Federal Reserve hike in December is also expected. That backdrop is pulling money into energy and insurers while growth-sensitive names lag.

Across the Atlantic the mood was less settled. Nvidia's leadership shock, which has wiped out nearly $1 trillion of value this month, weighed on US tech, yet the S&P 500 still rose 2.5% over the week. Asian chip stocks rallied anyway, and Europe had its best week since June.

World.title: US flight grounding and Trump's Asia summit dominate
World.notification: FAA lifts nationwide ground stop after nearly five hours; 6,700 flights cancelled
World.summary:
The FAA lifted a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday evening after nearly five hours of disruption. Officials blamed a telecommunications failure linked to outdated equipment and said there was no sign of a cyberattack. More than 6,700 flights were cancelled and over 25,000 delayed, and Transport Secretary Sean Duffy now says the air traffic control upgrade needs $50 billion, not $30 billion, renewing calls for emergency funding. Airline shares fell, with JetBlue, American and United among the weakest.

Abroad, the White House has confirmed Donald Trump will hold a trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin at the APEC summit in Shenzhen on 19 November. A senior US official said no agreement is expected, and the agenda covers nuclear arms and Iran but not Ukraine. It comes after New START expired in February, leaving no major arms control framework.

Europe is focused on Ukraine. EU leaders agreed a five-nation group, the E5, to represent Europe in future peace talks, a response to fears of a Yalta-style deal. In the UK, Prime Minister Andy Burnham says a "win-win" deal with the EU could be done before next week's summit.

Tech.title: Microsoft 365 outage hits Outlook and Teams worldwide
Tech.notification: Microsoft 365 outage knocks out Outlook and Teams worldwide as fixes stall
Tech.summary:
A global Microsoft 365 outage disrupted Outlook, Teams and other services on Friday 13 November, and Microsoft said its first fixes failed. The company blamed a process on affected servers that handles secure connections becoming overwhelmed, and it is rolling back a recent configuration change. Executive Charles Lamanna said there was no sign of malicious activity. In Australia, government agencies, courts and some clinics reported email problems, and authorities warned of scams exploiting the confusion.

The biggest new story in tech is therefore a reliability failure rather than a product launch. It shows how much of public-sector and business communication now depends on a single cloud provider. Microsoft's shares were down as a result.

Elsewhere, SpaceX's Starship flew its 15th test but the booster catch was aborted, leaving the double catch unfinished. The Ship continues in orbit, with a tower-catch decision expected on Saturday. Nvidia's leadership crisis also continues, with the chip-smuggling and China questions now reaching the White House.

Fashion.title: Capri names Boxford CEO as Idol retires
Fashion.notification: Capri names Estée Lauder veteran Justin Boxford as CEO, ending John Idol's 23-year run
Fashion.summary:
Capri Holdings, owner of Michael Kors and Jimmy Choo, has named Estée Lauder veteran Justin Boxford as chief executive from 4 January 2027, ending John Idol's long tenure. Idol retires as chairman and chief executive, and Robin Freestone becomes independent chairman. Boxford left Estée Lauder last week, and sources say Capri has been talking to potential acquirers about a sale.

Richemont dominates the rest of the week's luxury news. Its first-half sales rose 16% to €12.3 billion and operating profit climbed 33%, with jewellery leading. Yet shares fell nearly 4% on Friday, suggesting investors were wary of a slowing second quarter. Chairman Johann Rupert is also weighing whether to join a consortium bidding for a majority stake in De Beers.

Elsewhere, Hugo Boss confirmed that CEO Daniel Grieder will step down at the end of 2026, with Frasers-linked David Epstein taking over, while Bally's Italian units face liquidation.
